title: 'Early Dawn, the rosy-fingered'
greek: ἦμος δ᾽ ἠριγένεια φάνη ῥοδοδάκτυλος Ἠώς (ēmos d' ērigeneia phanē rhododaktylos Ēōs)
short: The most famous of Homer's time-formulas, marking a new day: Dawn, 'early-born', with fingers of rose.
body: This whole line recurs some twenty times in the Odyssey to open a new day (3.404, 3.491, 4.306, 4.431, 4.576 in these books alone). Merry and Riddell suggest that, beyond its place in the description of Eos as a beautiful woman, the epithet may picture the rays of rosy light that spread like the fingers of an open hand just before sunrise, an interpretation already found in Eustathius. Eos is cognate with Latin Aurora and Sanskrit Ushas, the dawn goddess of the Rig Veda. Ērigeneia means 'early-born' or 'born in the morning'. Such formulas are part of the traditional diction analysed by Milman Parry; they organize the narrative into days.

title: Aegyptius and his son Antiphus
greek: Αἰγύπτιος (Aigyptios)
short: The old man who opens the assembly has lost a son, Antiphus, to the Cyclops, a detail the audience understands but the Ithacans do not.
body: Aegyptius' son Antiphus sailed with Odysseus and was the last of the Cyclops' victims, his 'latest meal' (2.19-20; compare 9.344). The poet tells us this, though Aegyptius cannot know it: the old man still mourns him, while another son, Eurynomus, has joined the suitors. The detail links the Ithacan families to the fate of Odysseus' lost crews and quietly reminds us that Odysseus came home without any of the men he took. Several commentators also note the tension it sets up for the end of the poem, where the families of both the dead crewmen and the dead suitors are aggrieved against Odysseus (24.426-429). Aegyptius' wish that Zeus may fulfil the summoner's desire is taken by Telemachus as a good omen (2.35).

title: The Ithacan assembly (agorē) and council
greek: οὔτε ποθ᾽ ἡμετέρη ἀγορὴ γένετ᾽ οὔτε θόωκος (oute poth' hēmeterē agorē genet' oute thoōkos)
short: No assembly has met in Ithaca for twenty years; Telemachus, sitting in his father's seat, revives a public institution that has lapsed without its king.
body: The heralds summon the people, Telemachus enters with spear and dogs, and 'sat down in his father's seat, and the elders gave place'. Merry and Riddell explain that in the place of assembly the elders (gerontes) sat on stone seats in a sacred circle, as on the shield of Akhilleus (Iliad 18.503-504), and that Telemachus, as the king's son, takes the king's place. Thoōkos, 'session', means a meeting of the council of elders. Aegyptius' remark that there has been no assembly since Odysseus left shows how far public life has decayed in his absence. M. I. Finley used this scene as evidence for the limited political role of the Homeric assembly: it can be addressed and appealed to, but it votes on nothing, and here it fails to act.

title: Phēmē: the chance word taken as an omen
greek: χαῖρε δὲ φήμῃ Ὀδυσσῆος φίλος υἱός (chaire de phēmēi Odussēos philos huios)
short: Telemachus rejoices at Aegyptius' unwitting blessing: a casual utterance whose speaker does not know its full bearing was taken as a sign from the gods.
body: Merry and Riddell explain that the significance of a phēmē lies in its being spoken by chance: Aegyptius blesses the summoner of the assembly without knowing it is Telemachus, who only reveals himself at 2.40. The same belief appears in the related word klēdōn, used of the omens Odysseus receives before the slaughter (18.117; 20.100-121, where the two terms are used almost interchangeably). Such 'voices' are a recognised form of divination in Greek religion, alongside bird-signs; Athena mentions 'a voice from Zeus, which oftenest brings tidings to men' at 1.282-283. The motif structures the poem's second half, where chance words and sneezes (17.541-547) foretell the suitors' doom.

anchor: staff was placed in his hands
title: The speaker's staff (skēptron)
greek: σκῆπτρον δέ οἱ ἔμβαλε χειρὶ κῆρυξ Πεισήνωρ (skēptron de hoi embale cheiri kēryx Peisēnōr)
short: The herald puts the staff in Telemachus' hand: holding the skēptron gives a speaker the right to address the assembly.
body: Merry and Riddell note that the staff was the badge of public office, carried by kings (3.412), priests (Iliad 1.15), prophets (11.91), heralds and judges; when the herald placed it in a speaker's hand in assembly, he gave him a temporary public authority. Telemachus ends his speech by dashing the staff to the ground in tears (2.80-81), a gesture that recalls Akhilleus throwing down the sceptre in his quarrel with Agamemnon (Iliad 1.245-246). The echo marks Telemachus' anger, but also his helplessness: the pity of the people produces no action. Nestor too sits 'holding a sceptre in his hands' before his palace (3.412).

title: The good king 'gentle as a father'
greek: πατὴρ δ᾽ ὣς ἤπιος ἦεν (patēr d' hōs ēpios ēen)
short: Odysseus ruled Ithaca 'gentle as a father': the poem's ideal of kingship, used by Telemachus and Mentor and repeated by Athena on Olympus.
body: Telemachus says his father was king 'and was gentle as a father' (2.47); Mentor repeats the phrase in his bitter speech that kings might as well be harsh, since no one remembers Odysseus' kindness (2.230-234), and Athena uses Mentor's very words among the gods (5.8-12). Merry and Riddell explain the clause at 2.234 as concessive, 'though he was mild as a father'. Penelope's later description of Odysseus as a ruler who never wronged anyone in word or deed, unlike most kings (4.687-693), develops the same theme. The ideal of the king as benevolent father stands against the suitors' exploitation of his house and against the people's passivity, which Mentor attacks directly.

title: Themis, goddess of right order
greek: Ζηνὸς Ὀλυμπίου ἠδὲ Θέμιστος, ἥ τ᾽ ἀνδρῶν ἀγορὰς ἠμὲν λύει ἠδὲ καθίζει (Zēnos Olympiou ēde Themistos, hē t' andrōn agoras ēmen luei ēde kathizei)
short: Telemachus appeals to Zeus and to Themis, the personification of established right, who presides over the opening and closing of assemblies.
body: Themis means 'that which is laid down': custom, right, the proper order of things; the plural themistes means traditional judgments. As a goddess she is Zeus' companion (in Hesiod, Theogony 901, his second wife) and in the Iliad she summons the gods to assembly (Iliad 20.4) and greets Hera at the feast (Iliad 15.87-95). Telemachus' appeal therefore invokes the very order the suitors are violating: the assembly exists to uphold what is right, and the people should act. His speech also asks the Ithacans to fear 'the wrath of the gods' and the judgement of their neighbours, appealing to both divine and social sanctions. Hugh Lloyd-Jones discusses themis and dikē as the moral vocabulary of Homer's world.

title: 'The well-greaved Achaeans'
greek: ἐυκνήμιδας Ἀχαιούς (euknēmidas Achaious)
short: A stock epithet of the Greeks as warriors: they wear fine greaves (knēmides), shin-guards of bronze or leather.
body: Greaves protected the leg from knee to ankle and appear in the arming scenes of the Iliad (for example Iliad 3.330-331). Bronze greaves have been found in Mycenaean graves (for instance at Dendra) and were standard hoplite equipment in later centuries, so the epithet is not tied to a single period, a point often made about Homer's armour. In the Odyssey the formula survives even in peaceful contexts: Athena calls Telemachus' young rowers 'well-greaved comrades' (2.402), though they are sailing, not fighting. Here Telemachus asks whether his father ever wronged 'the well-greaved Achaeans', so that the Ithacans are taking revenge on the son.

title: Penelope's web: the shroud for Laertes
greek: στησαμένη μέγαν ἱστὸν ἐνὶ μεγάροισιν ὕφαινε (stēsamenē megan histon eni megaroisin huphaine)
short: Penelope promised to choose a husband when she finished a shroud for Laertes, wove by day and unravelled by night for three years, until a maid betrayed her.
body: Antinous tells the story as an accusation, but it shows Penelope's mētis ('cunning intelligence'), which matches her husband's. Merry and Riddell explain that setting up the histos means stretching the warp on the upright loom; the epithets 'fine and very wide' indicate how long the work would take. The pretext is pious: a shroud (taphēion) for her father-in-law, so that the women of the land should not blame her if he lay without one. The story is told three times, by Antinous here, by Penelope herself to the disguised Odysseus (19.137-156), and by the ghost of the suitor Amphimedon in the Underworld (24.128-146), each time from a different angle. Weaving and unweaving have become a central image for readers of the poem: Penelope delays time itself while waiting. Murnaghan and Katz discuss how the trick defines her.

title: Tyro, Alcmene and Mycene: heroines of old
greek: Τυρώ τ᾽ Ἀλκμήνη τε ἐυστέφανός τε Μυκήνη (Tyrō t' Alkmēnē te eustephanos te Mukēnē)
short: Antinous compares Penelope with famous women of legend and says none matched her in cunning.
body: Merry and Riddell identify the three: Tyro, daughter of Salmoneus, mother (by Poseidon) of Neleus and Pelias, and so grandmother of Nestor; Alcmene, mother of Heracles by Zeus; and Mycene, daughter of Inachus according to the Hesiodic Great Ehoiai, who gave her name to the city of Mycenae. Tyro and Alcmene reappear among the heroines Odysseus sees in the Underworld (11.235-259, 11.266-268). The list belongs to the genre of catalogues of women, best known from the fragmentary Hesiodic Catalogue of Women. The compliment is double-edged: Antinous praises Penelope's wits, 'yet this at least she devised not aright', because her delay is ruining her son's estate while winning her 'great fame' (kleos).

title: Sending Penelope home to Icarius
greek: κακὸν δέ με πόλλ᾽ ἀποτίνειν Ἰκαρίῳ (kakon de me poll' apotinein Ikariōi)
short: Telemachus refuses to send his mother back to her father, Icarius: it would cost him a heavy penalty, the father's anger and the mother's curse.
body: The suitors want Penelope returned to her father's house so that he can give her in marriage (2.52-54, 2.113-114). Telemachus says that if he sent her away against her will he would have to 'pay back much' to Icarius. Many readers take this as returning her dowry. Merry and Riddell reject that: they argue (in their note on 1.277) that hedna came from the groom, not the bride's father, and so take the phrase as a general penalty Icarius would exact for the insult to his daughter. They report an ancient punctuation that avoids making Telemachus sound mercenary. Either way, the passage shows that Penelope's legal position is ambiguous: neither widow nor wife, she cannot be disposed of by her son. In later tradition Icarius is the brother of Tyndareus, which makes Penelope a cousin of Helen and Clytemnestra.

title: The Erinyes (Furies)
greek: μήτηρ στυγερὰς ἀρήσετ᾽ ἐρινῦς (mētēr stugeras arēset' erinus)
short: The Erinyes are the powers that punish wrongs within the family, above all against parents; a mother driven from her house would call them down on her son.
body: Merry and Riddell describe the Erinyes as agents of the gods below (Hades and Persephone, Iliad 9.453-457), avengers of perjury (Iliad 19.259-260) and executors of a parent's curse (here and at 11.280), so that the word can even stand for the curse itself. They also protect the old and the beggar (Iliad 15.204; Odyssey 17.475). Their office is the punishment of crimes against family and society. The etymology is unknown; Merry and Riddell report several proposals. In Aeschylus' Eumenides they pursue Orestes for killing his mother, a story the Odyssey's version of Orestes passes over in silence.

title: The omen of the two eagles
greek: τῷ δ᾽ αἰετὼ εὐρύοπα Ζεὺς ὑψόθεν ἐκ κορυφῆς ὄρεος προέηκε πέτεσθαι (tōi d' aietō euruopa Zeus hupsothen ek koruphēs oreos proeēke petesthai)
short: Zeus 'whose voice is borne afar' sends two eagles that glare down on the assembly, tear each other and fly off right: a sign of death for the suitors.
body: Eagles are Zeus' birds, and a sign on the right was favourable. The birds look down 'and death was in their glare', a vivid image of violence descending on the gathering. Halitherses reads the omen as Odysseus' return and the suitors' destruction (2.161-176). The epithet euryopa Zeus, here rendered 'whose voice is borne afar', is ambiguous: Merry and Riddell note that ancient interpreters already offered both 'far-seeing' and 'far-sounding' (the thunder as Zeus' voice) and incline to the latter while acknowledging the difficulty. Bird omens recur through the poem, always pointing to vengeance (15.160-178, 19.535-553, 20.242-243). The scene answers Zeus' warning speech in Book 1: the suitors, like Aegisthus, are told.

title: Halitherses the seer
greek: Ἁλιθέρσης Μαστορίδης … ὄρνιθας γνῶναι καὶ ἐναίσιμα μυθήσασθαι (Halithersēs Mastoridēs … ornithas gnōnai kai enaisima muthēsasthai)
short: The old seer, unrivalled in reading birds, interprets the eagles as Odysseus' return and recalls his prophecy that Odysseus would come home in the twentieth year, unknown to all.
body: Halitherses has the gift of reading birds and of 'uttering words of fate'. He reminds the assembly that when the fleet sailed for Troy he foretold that Odysseus, after losing all his comrades, would return in the twentieth year unrecognized (2.174-176), which is exactly what the poem will show. Eurymachus answers with sneering scepticism (2.178-207): many birds fly under the sun and not all are fateful. The exchange is one of the clearest examples of the warning that the doomed ignore, the pattern announced in Zeus' first speech. Halitherses speaks again at the end of the poem, trying to stop the suitors' kinsmen from attacking Odysseus (24.451-462). His father's name, Mastor ('Seeker'), suits a diviner.

title: Mentor, and Athena in his likeness
greek: Μέντωρ, ὅς ῥ᾽ Ὀδυσῆος ἀμύμονος ἦεν ἑταῖρος (Mentōr, hos rh' Odusēos amumonos ēen hetairos)
short: Mentor, Odysseus' old friend left in charge of his house, speaks in the assembly; afterwards Athena repeatedly takes his form to guide Telemachus.
body: Merry and Riddell point out that this is the only passage in which Mentor appears in his own person; elsewhere it is Athena impersonating him (2.267-268, 2.401, Books 3, 22 and 24). They also note the likeness of his name to Mentes, Athena's first disguise. Odysseus 'gave all his house in charge' to Mentor, though Merry and Riddell, quoting Hayman at 3.267, observe that his commission covered the house and goods, not Penelope. Through the French writer Fénelon's novel Les Aventures de Télémaque (1699), in which Minerva as Mentor educates the young Telemachus, the name became the English common noun 'mentor', a wise adviser. The poem itself plays on the idea: as Mentor, Athena teaches Telemachus how to speak, act and pray.

title: Washing before prayer
greek: χεῖρας νιψάμενος πολιῆς ἁλὸς εὔχετ᾽ Ἀθήνῃ (cheiras nipsamenos poliēs halos euchet' Athēnēi)
short: Telemachus goes alone to the shore, washes his hands in the sea and prays to Athena: ritual purity was required before approaching a god.
body: Merry and Riddell compare the Achaeans purifying themselves and throwing the defilement into the sea before a sacrifice to Apollo (Iliad 1.313-316) and Priam washing his hands before a libation (Iliad 24.302-306). Polios, 'grey', is the regular epithet of the sea near the shore, where it is whitened by foam. Telemachus' prayer recalls the visitor of yesterday and asks for help; Athena answers at once in the form of Mentor. Telemachus will pray again at the end of the book with libations (2.430-433), and Penelope prays to Athena after washing and putting on clean clothes (4.750-767), a sequence that shows the household turning to the goddess.

title: 'Few sons are like their fathers'
greek: παῦροι γάρ τοι παῖδες ὁμοῖοι πατρὶ πέλονται, οἱ πλέονες κακίους, παῦροι δέ τε πατρὸς ἀρείους (pauroi gar toi paides homoioi patri pelontai …)
short: Athena-as-Mentor states a pessimistic maxim, 'most sons are worse, few better', and then assures Telemachus that he has his father's spirit.
body: The maxim reflects a common Greek belief in the decline of generations, found also in Nestor's talk of the stronger men of old (Iliad 1.260-272) and in Hesiod's myth of the ages (Works and Days 109-201). Athena uses it as a challenge: 'if thou art not the son of him and of Penelope', she would have no hope. The poem's answer is that Telemachus will prove a worthy son, and in the final book Laertes rejoices to see son and grandson vying in courage (24.514-515). The speech belongs to the chain of passages on likeness between father and son that begins with Telemachus' own doubt at 1.215-216.

title: Barley meal, 'the marrow of men'
greek: ἄλφιτα, μυελὸν ἀνδρῶν (alphita, muelon andrōn)
short: Barley meal is called 'the marrow of men', the food that gives men their strength.
body: Alphita is barley groats or meal, the staple of Homeric provisions, packed in leather bags for voyages; Telemachus asks Eurycleia for twenty measures (2.354-355). The metaphor reflects the belief that marrow (muelos) was the seat of life and strength in the body; food that keeps a man strong can thus be called his marrow. The phrase recurs at 20.108, where a weary woman grinding barley at the mill curses the suitors who have worn out her knees with the labour of making 'the marrow of men'. Wine is stored in jars (amphiphoreis) and the two are the basic stores for Telemachus' journey.

title: Diogenēs, 'Zeus-born'
greek: διογενὴς Ὀδυσεύς (diogenēs Odusseus)
short: An honorific epithet of kings and heroes, 'sprung from Zeus', marking their status rather than literal descent.
body: Odysseus' genealogy (Laertes, Arceisius) does not make him a literal son of Zeus, although later tradition traced Arceisius to Zeus. Diogenēs belongs with diotrephēs, 'fostered by Zeus' (Murray's 'fostered of Zeus', used of Menelaus at 4.26 and elsewhere), and with dios, 'godlike, brilliant'. These epithets express the Homeric view that kings hold their honour from Zeus (compare Iliad 2.196-197, 2.205-206). Eurycleia uses the formula in her grief, imagining that Odysseus has perished 'in a strange land' (2.365-366), and Telemachus hopes he may come home 'having escaped from death and the fates'. Arceisius appears in Book 4 (4.755).

title: Eurycleia's oath
greek: γρῆυς δὲ θεῶν μέγαν ὅρκον ἀπώμνυ (grēus de theōn megan horkon apōmnu)
short: Eurycleia swears 'the great oath of the gods' to keep Telemachus' departure secret for eleven or twelve days.
body: Merry and Riddell note that 'great oath of the gods' can mean either an oath by the gods, as the context requires here, or the oath the gods themselves swear, by the water of Styx (Homeric Hymn to Demeter 259; Hesiod, Theogony 784-806). They discuss the force of the prefix in apōmnu, either 'swore that she would not' or 'swore in due form', followed by 'made an end of the oath' (2.378). Oaths in Homer are binding under divine sanction; breaking one brings the Erinyes (Iliad 19.259-260). Eurycleia keeps her word, and when Penelope discovers her son's absence the nurse confesses and explains the oath (4.742-749).

title: Athena disguised as Telemachus
greek: Τηλεμάχῳ ἐικυῖα κατὰ πτόλιν ᾤχετο πάντῃ (Tēlemachōi eikuia kata ptolin ōicheto pantēi)
short: Athena takes the shape of Telemachus himself to recruit a crew, borrows a ship from Noemon, and then puts the suitors to sleep: the goddess runs the whole expedition.
body: This is Athena's third disguise in two books (Mentes, Mentor, Telemachus), and the only time she impersonates the hero she is helping. She gathers the rowers, borrows a ship from Noemon son of Phronius, drags it to the sea at nightfall, and sheds sleep on the suitors so that they leave the hall early (2.393-398). The repeated phrase 'took other counsel' (2.382, 2.393) marks her initiatives. The episode shows the scale of divine management in the Telemachy and has a later consequence: Noemon's innocent enquiry about his ship (4.630-656), together with his report that he saw 'Mentor, or a god', alerts the suitors to the journey and sets off their ambush. His name and his father's, 'Thinker son of Sensible', are speaking names.

title: Rigging the ship: mast, stays and sail
greek: ἱστὸν δ᾽ εἰλάτινον κοίλης ἔντοσθε μεσόδμης στῆσαν ἀείραντες, κατὰ δὲ προτόνοισιν ἔδησαν (histon d' eilatinon koilēs entosthe mesodmēs …)
short: A compact sailing scene: the crew raise the fir mast into its box, fasten the forestays and hoist the white sail as a west wind fills it.
body: Merry and Riddell explain the 'hollow socket' (koilē mesodmē) as the mast-box, a structure that enclosed the foot of the mast so that it could be raised and lowered, and discuss the detail in their appendix on the Homeric ship. Protonoi are the forestays running from mast-head to bow. The fir (eilatē) was valued for masts and oars. Athena sends a 'strong-blowing West wind' (akraē Zephyron, 2.421), favourable for a run south from Ithaca to Pylos. The lines form a typical sailing scene, repeated with variations elsewhere (for example 15.287-292); the sound of the wave 'singing' about the stem is one of the poem's fine touches of seafaring realism.

anchor: poured libations to the immortal gods
title: Libations at sea
greek: στήσαντο κρητῆρας ἐπιστεφέας οἴνοιο, λεῖβον δ᾽ ἀθανάτοισι θεοῖς (stēsanto krētēras epistepheas oinoio, leibon d' athanatoisi theois)
short: Once under way, the crew set out mixing-bowls 'brim-full of wine' and pour offerings to all the gods, above all to Athena.
body: A libation (loibē, spondē) was the pouring of a little wine for the gods before drinking, and accompanied prayer, departure and oath. Merry and Riddell discuss the phrase 'bowls brim-full' (epistepheas, literally 'crowned') and Virgil's imitation 'crateras magnos statuunt et vina coronant' (Aeneid 1.724), which they suspect misunderstands the Greek by taking the 'crown' as a garland. The crew honours 'chiefest of all the flashing-eyed daughter of Zeus', not knowing that she is sitting in the stern beside Telemachus. Libations recur at Pylos (3.40-64, 3.332-342) and are a basic act of Homeric piety.
